source.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Michael Lan; P. Torr; Austin Meek; Ashkan Khakzar; David Krueger; Fazl Barez

record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE feature-space similarity and reproducibility in LLMs using activation matching plus SVCCA/RSA, rather than testing the original toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition and polysemanticity as background but does not test capacity pressure, sparsity-dependent transitions, importance-dependent geometry, or feature dropping in toy networks. Its own results relevant here concern SAE feature spaces in LLMs and how consistently SAEs capture them. Cited findings and the paper's background discussion are not recorded as result rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's main results concern cross-model universality of SAE feature-space geometry, which no version names. Its appendix results on SAEs trained with different seeds, widths and datasets do bear on V5, and the authors explicitly conclude that SAEs do not capture features consistently.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SAE feature subspaces, especially in middle layers and for some semantic concepts, are highly similar across LLMs under rotation-invariant measures, which they read as evidence of 'weakly universal' features. They add that a notable fraction of features is idiosyncratic to particular SAEs and that SAEs do not capture these features consistently; they explicitly do not claim that SAEs learn the same features.
record.recipe_differences: The original source uses toy models to study superposition geometry. This study uses pretrained LLMs and SAE decoder weights, activation-correlation pairing, SVCCA, and RSA to compare feature-space relations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with layer, semantic concept, SAE training quality and seed, dataset, feature width, pairing direction, and filtering choices. The authors note that middle layers generally score highest, some concepts or layers do not match, and feature pairing quality affects the measures.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE feature spaces of different LLMs (Pythia, Gemma, Llama), once paired by activation correlation, show SVCCA/RSA similarity far above random pairing, highest in middle layers. This also holds for several semantic subspaces; Gemma 'Countries' fails Test 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model universality of SAE feature-space geometry (analogous feature universality).

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on a randomized Pythia-70m show very low similarity to SAEs trained on the real model, with about 1% of pairs retained (Appendix D, Fig 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature-space similarity reflects trained model structure rather than data sparsity alone.

record.problems: The study compares only a sample of SAEs and LLMs with the same tokenizer; activation datasets are limited in size. It does not measure ground-truth features or how well models capture them, and its similarity results depend on SAE quality, feature pairing, and filtering. The authors note that SAE features can be inconsistent and that generalizability to other datasets and specialized models remains open.
record.rows_left_out: Not all individual layer-pair score cells from the many plotted matrices in Figures 2-18 and Appendices M and related figures are listed separately. The record includes text-level aggregate results, highlighted layer comparisons, and the tabulated semantic-subspace values; the remaining plotted layer-pair matrices are omitted because they are extensive and largely repeat the same comparisons.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry analysis.
All: capacity or importance allocation is not studied.
All: no alternative mechanisms for polysemanticity.
Not measured quantitatively. Only an unquantified remark that most LLM neurons checked were polysemantic (Appendix L).
Completeness and canonicality against ground-truth units. Per-feature identity across seeds is not directly measured; only paired-subspace similarity is.
All: dimensionality of features is not tested.

missing.what: TinyStories seed SAEs paired by cosine similarity: mean cosine 0.9, SVCCA 0.92, and every feature finds a unique pair but no exact matches.
TinyStories seed SAEs at expansion factor 8: SVCCA 0.84/0.87 before filtering, 0.94 after.
Same-SAE cross-layer similarity differs between the Eleuther 8.2B-token SAEs and the custom 100M-token SAEs (e.g. the L5 vs L1 pair).
RedPajama- vs OpenWebText-trained SAEs on Pythia-70m show both similarities and dissimilarities.
Unquantified check that the majority of LLM neurons are polysemantic (top 90 samples).
missing.locator: Appendix L, end of the paragraph after Table 3

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the cross-model universality rows to V4, but universality is a different construct, so those rows were moved to fits_no_version and V4 counts as untested. V5 evidence comes only from the appendix comparisons across seeds, widths and datasets, measured at the level of paired subspaces after filtering non-concept features, which inflates scores. This study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, interference, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises through other mechanisms without capacity pressure.
The study measures SAE feature-space relations, not the full distribution of a model's features across its neurons or the completeness of SAE recovery.
It examines consistency across some SAEs and settings, but does not establish completeness or canonicality against ground-truth model units.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m SAEs trained with different seeds
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE feature-space mappings across different training seeds using SVCCA.
rows.baseline: Same SAE compared with itself has similarity 1
rows.note: The authors say the different-seed results resemble some same-SAE comparisons but have notable differences, consistent with SAEs not learning consistent features.
rows.check: State is right. Note the comparison is to a same-SAE baseline of 1, and random pairing is about 0.01. Seed stability is well above chance but far from identical, and the authors say the SAEs do not find the same features.

rows.note: The score concerns mapped feature-space similarity, not whether the SAE features are complete, canonical, or individually identical.
rows.check: This does bear on V5 seed stability: a 1-layer model, SVCCA of 0.94 against a random baseline of 0.004. Note it is after filtering, and is subspace-level, not per-feature identity.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m SAE comparisons across training datasets
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE feature-space similarity for SAEs trained on different datasets.
rows.measure: Paired SVCCA and RSA feature-space similarity
rows.value: The authors report both similarities and notable dissimilarities across layer comparisons, including nearly no similarity at Layers 2 and 4; they state that the compared feature subspaces appear highly similar overall.
rows.note: The authors suggest dataset differences may contribute to discrepancies and state that SAEs are dataset dependent.
rows.check: Correct. SAEs trained on different datasets show nearly no similarity at layers 2 and 4 but some at layers 1, 3 and 5. Only 4.58% of pairs are retained.

rows.check: 'No noticeable trends' with width cannot show stability or instability; no scores are summarized.

rows.subject: Custom Pythia-70m and Pythia-160m SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of feature pairs retained in comparisons involving custom-trained SAEs.

conditions.value: custom-trained SAEs versus pretrained Eleuther and SAELens SAEs

rows.measure: Percentage of feature pairs retained after filtering
rows.value: Around 2 to 4% retained on average for custom-trained SAEs
rows.note: The authors attribute the lower retained fraction to custom SAEs capturing features less well, while noting the difference in SAE training-token counts.
rows.check: Retained-pair fraction depends on SAE training tokens (100M vs 8.2B). This is about SAE quality and only indirectly about stability.

source_check.correct: Experiments using custom-trained SAEs retain around 2–4% of feature pairs; experiments using pretrained Eleuther and SAELens SAEs retain 20–30%. These are groups of experiments, not exclusively custom-versus-pretrained comparisons. State for V5: cannot_determine from retained-pair fractions alone.
source_check.problem: The comparison condition misstates the experiment groups, and retained-pair fractions alone do not establish completeness, stability or canonicality.
